title: When do Godement–Jacquet and Rankin–Selberg conductors coincide?
question:
Let F be a non-archimedean local field, let Pi (resp. pi) be a generic representation of GL_n(F) (resp. GL_m(F)), and fix an additive character psi of conductor O_F. The Godement--Jacquet integral gives a conductor exponent c_{\mathrm{GJ}}(Pi \times pi)=c(Pi)+c(pi), while the Rankin--Selberg integral in the Whittaker model produces its own exponent via the epsilon factor \varepsilon(s,Pi \times pi,\psi)=\omega(Pi \times pi,\psi)\,q^{-c_{\mathrm{RS}}(Pi \times pi)(s-\tfrac12)}. Take W_0 to be the Casselman new vector of Pi satisfying W_0(gk)=W_0(g) for k \in K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(Pi)}).

How can one prove that the RS exponent c_{\mathrm{RS}}(Pi \times pi) equals the GJ exponent once one translates W_0 by any unipotent element u_Q, and why does this identification force conductor matching and the expected nonvanishing statements for R(u_Q)W_0? I am especially interested in the role of the support description from the Casselman--Shalika formula and the way the epsilon factor constraints enforce the equality.
answer:
Start with the Godement--Jacquet construction. Choosing Casselman new vectors v_0 for Pi and w_0 for pi means the matrix coefficient used in the GJ zeta integral is fixed by K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(Pi)}) \times K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(pi)}). The Bruhat–Schwartz function in the integral can thus be chosen to detect only those cosets, and the local functional equation shows that the resulting conductor exponent equals the valuation of the product of the two newform conductors, namely c_{\mathrm{GJ}}(Pi \times pi)=c(Pi)+c(pi).

For the Rankin--Selberg integral, transfer v_0 to its Whittaker model as W_0. Casselman–Shalika tells us W_0 is supported in N(F)T^{+}K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(Pi)}), with nonzero values on every dominant torus element. If u_Q ranges through the unipotent representatives of K_1(\mathfrak{p}^{c(pi)}), JPSS (1981, §5) shows that R(u_Q)W_0 remains in the same support region and never vanishes: the right translation merely modifies the N-component, leaving the torus valuation unchanged. Therefore the RS integral with W_0 and the new vector W_{pi} of pi picks up the same q-adic contributions as the GJ integral, so the conductor detected by Rankin--Selberg also equals c(Pi)+c(pi).

Finally, the local epsilon factor is normalized by the functional equation \varepsilon(s,Pi \times pi,\psi)=\omega(Pi \times pi,\psi)\,q^{-c_{\mathrm{RS}}(Pi \times pi)(s-\tfrac12)}. Because the change of variables argument above expresses every RS integral in terms of the GJ newform integral, the same epsilon factor is also \omega q^{-c_{\mathrm{GJ}}(Pi \times pi)(s-1/2)}. Equality of the gamma factors forces c_{\mathrm{RS}}=c_{\mathrm{GJ}} and simultaneously shows R(u_Q)W_0 \neq 0 for all Q. Thus the conductor matching and epsilon factor constraints are satisfied precisely when one works with Casselman new vectors and the unipotent translates that preserve their support.

if W_0 is the Casselman new vector then R(u_Q)W_0 \neq 0
